F5/F6: detect a struggling consumer. Multiple valid tool paths — list-queues exposes the F5 queue backing up, list-slow-subscribers/list-clients expose the F6 client whose slowSubscriber flag is set. Accept any; assert both fixtures surface in the answer.

This row carried a forbidden_substrings deny-list until SOL-153377. Its stated purpose was to stop an echo-the-name refusal passing on required_substrings alone, which stopped applying once the prompt no longer named the queue: the agent cannot echo a name it was never given, so an answer containing $F5_QUEUE has already read it off the broker. What the deny-list kept doing was flag correct answers. 'no queues' and 'zero queues' went first — the suite provisions test-vpn-empty as a bare VPN, so an agent that enumerates VPNs reports one has no queues as a matter of fact. Then the all-clear needles ('nothing struggling', 'none struggling') did the same thing to 'Nothing struggling in test-vpn-empty', a true statement about the empty VPN sitting next to a correct detection in the default one. Both times a substring could not see the scope the sentence was qualified by.

The replacement is positive evidence instead of absence of a phrase: name the specific client the broker flagged. $F6_SUB_CLIENT_NAME_A is discoverable only from the slowSubscriber signal — it is in no prompt in this suite and in no queue listing — so an answer that names it has done the detection, and an all-clear verdict cannot produce it by accident. That closes the same gap without any wording assumption to go stale.

Cost of the trade: this now requires the agent to reach the client-level signal, not just the queue. A run that stops at list-queues answers the question defensibly and still goes red. That is the intended strictness for this row — 'which consumer' is the answer the fixture exists to test — but it is the first thing to reconsider if the row starts flaking on model updates.
prompt: Are any consumers on $BROKER struggling to keep up right now?
